subject: english-literature
title: Big Ideas in Books
welcome_lead: Friendship, courage, family — meet the themes you'll see again and again.
meta_desc: KS3 English Literature adventure on common themes in stories.
final_note: You can now name and trace several common literary themes.

concepts.def: Big idea explored by a story.
Bravery in the face of fear.
Bonds of blood or chosen kin.
Move from child to adult ideas.

walkthroughs.body_html: From The Outsiders to Harry Potter, friendship tests loyalty, trust and forgiveness — a key KS3 theme.
Courage doesn't mean fearless — it means acting despite fear. Watch for moments characters choose to act bravely.
Stories about growing up (Bildungsroman) trace a young hero gaining understanding — like Pip in Great Expectations.

Acting despite fear

Foreshadowing is the shadow a character casts in a scene.
Subtle hints or clues earlier in a text that anticipate later events, making the resolution feel both surprising and inevitable.
The speaker is whoever reads the poem out loud.
Foreshadowing is when a character predicts the future.

mcqs.q: Why distinguish the speaker of a poem from the poet?
options: The speaker is whoever reads the poem out loud.
The speaker is the voice constructed in the poem; the poet is the writer. Treating them as identical can mislead, especially with dramatic monologues or personae.
Foreshadowing is the shadow a character casts in a scene.
The speaker of a poem is always the poet themselves.
When a speaker says one thing but means another — typically the opposite — relying on shared context for the listener to detect the gap.
The speaker is whoever reads the poem out loud.
Verbal irony is just saying something unexpected.
Verbal irony is when you make a joke about something.
